abstract.title: ABSTRACT
abstract.p: TAK‐500 is a novel immune cell–directed antibody–drug conjugate (iADC) composed of TAK‐202, an anti‐CCR2 monoclonal antibody, conjugated to the STING agonist dazostinag (TAK‐676), and is designed to stimulate antitumor immunity by reprogramming CCR2‐positive monocytes. To support clinical translation, we developed a population pharmacokinetic (PK)–receptor occupancy (RO) model that leveraged both preclinical and clinical data from the parental antibody. In cynomolgus monkeys, TAK‐500 displayed nonlinear, target‐mediated disposition with dose‐dependent CCR2 RO and monocyte redistribution. A 2‐compartment PK model confirmed that TAK‐500 total antibody and TAK‐202 exhibited comparable PK profiles in monkeys, suggesting translational concordance. In humans, TAK‐202 demonstrated nonlinear PK with greater‐than‐dose‐proportional exposure, which was not captured by allometric scaling from monkeys but provided a critical basis for model development. We established a population PK–RO model of TAK‐202 in humans and integrated it with cynomolgus TAK‐500 data to project human PK and RO across doses of 50–500 μg/kg. Simulations (n = 1000) predicted dose‑dependent decreases in clearance, from 40 to 31 mL/h for total antibody and from 148 to 124 mL/h for conjugated payload (median values in a 70‑kg adult), respectively. Corresponding terminal half‐lives were estimated at 114–118 h for total antibody and 30–60 h for conjugated payload. These findings demonstrate the feasibility of predicting TAK‐500 PK and RO in humans by integrating preclinical and parental antibody clinical data, providing a quantitative framework for first‐in‐human dose selection of immune cell–directed ADCs.
Trial Registration: Clinical trials: NCT04420884, NCT04879849

list-item.p:
What is the current knowledge on the topic? ○
Antibody–drug conjugates (ADCs) typically rely on tumor antigen expression for activity, yet many solid tumors develop resistance through antigen loss or heterogeneity. Immune cell–directed ADCs represent a novel approach to overcome this limitation by targeting nonmalignant cells in the tumor microenvironment. TAK‐500 is an immune cell–directed ADC that couples the anti‐CCR2 antibody TAK‐202 with a STING agonist payload, designed to reprogram immunosuppressive myeloid cells.

What question did this study address? ○
This study sought to characterize the pharmacokinetics (PK), receptor occupancy (RO), and pharmacodynamics (PD) of TAK‐500 in cynomolgus monkeys and to build a translational population PK–PD model leveraging both preclinical monkey data and clinical data of the parental antibody TAK‐202 to predict TAK‐500 PK–RO relationships in humans.

What does this study add to our knowledge? ○
TAK‐500 exhibited nonlinear, target‐mediated PK, dose‐dependent CCR2 engagement, and monocyte redistribution in cynomolgus monkeys. A mechanistic model integrating antibody disposition, receptor binding, and payload deconjugation was successfully translated to humans by anchoring to clinical TAK‐202 data. Model predictions indicated nonlinear TAK‐500 PK in humans across the projected therapeutic dose range, with distinct half‐lives for the antibody backbone and conjugated payload.

How might this change clinical pharmacology or translational science? ○
This work demonstrates the feasibility of predicting human PK and RO of immune cell–directed ADCs by integrating preclinical and parental antibody clinical data. The approach provides a rational framework for first‐in‐human dose selection and may accelerate the development of next‐generation ADCs that reprogram the tumor microenvironment.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Antibody‐drug conjugates (ADCs) are an important class of anticancer agents that combine the target specificity of monoclonal antibodies (mAb) with highly cytotoxic small molecule drugs (payloads) to achieve anti‐tumor efficacy with acceptable toxicity profiles. A growing number of ADCs have been approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) in recent years for the treatment of both haemopoietic and solid tumors [1]. These ADCs share a common mechanism of action that relies on overexpressed tumor surface antigens to enrich the conjugates in the tumor, followed by internalization and endo‐lysosomal protease cleavage to ultimately deliver a highly cytotoxic payload. The prerequisite of overexpressed tumor antigens limits ADCs to certain cancer populations and may render them prone to tumor resistance due to altered antigen presentation after treatment. An emerging class of ADCs, called immune cell‐directed antibody‐drug conjugates (iADCs), is being developed to modulate the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME), with multiple candidates currently evaluated both preclinically and in early stages of development. Such an approach, if successful, may benefit cancer patients regardless of their tumor antigen presentation and may achieve synergies when combined with other cancer therapeutics, including immune checkpoint inhibitors [2].

TAK‐500 is a novel immune stimulatory ADC comprising a STING agonist (dazostinag or TAK‐676, which is currently in phase 1/2 clinical trials), an anti‐cysteine chemokine receptor 2 (CCR2) antibody (TAK‐202) with an effectorless IgG1 Fc, and a self‐immolating maleimide‐containing protease‐cleavable peptide linker [3]. TAK‐500 has an average drug‐to‐antibody ratio (DAR) of 4.0. CCR2 is expressed on monocytes and other immune subsets of cells and is known to play an important role in recruiting monocytes/macrophages to the TME. These myeloid cells, including tumor‐associated macrophages (TAMs), promote an immune suppressive TME. Upon binding and internalization of TAK‐500 to CCR2‐expressing myeloid cells, TAK‐676 is released and activates STING/interferon pathway signaling, resulting in a type I interferon (IFN)‐mediated response that potentially reprograms immunosuppressive myeloid cells in the TME [4]. TAK‐500 has the potential to stimulate innate and adaptive immunity in the TME through activation of IFN signaling, reprogramming of CCR2‐expressing myeloid cells to an inflammatory phenotype, and blockade of suppressive TAM recruitment, thus mitigating tumor resistance to checkpoint inhibitors [3, 5]. TAK‐500 is terminated in phase 1/2 clinical trial as a single agent and in combination with pembrolizumab in patients with advanced solid tumors (NCT05070247).

Preclinical development of TAK‐500 included pharmacokinetic (PK) and pharmacodynamic (PD) characterization in cynomolgus monkeys to project human PK and facilitate clinical dose selection. A recent retrospective analysis by Li et al. [6], with 11 ADCs, demonstrated that the human clearance (CL) of both conjugated payload and total antibody is best captured by allometrically scaling CL from nonhuman primate alone with an exponent of 1.0. Moreover, as the difference in CL between the conjugated payload and the total antibody often reflects linker stability, the good agreement of nonhuman primate and human CL for both conjugated payload and total antibody suggests that ADC linker stability in humans can be estimated from nonhuman primate PK studies. However, the retrospective analysis was limited to ADCs that exhibit linear PK in the clinical dose range, and human PK prediction of ADCs with nonlinear PK due to target‐mediated drug disposition (TMDD) remains challenging. This is because species differences in target expression levels and turnover, as well as antibody interaction (e.g., binding affinity, Kd, kon, or koff) with the target, need to be considered [7]. Additionally, ADC tolerability in cynomolgus monkeys often limits a wide dose range PK study in order to capture target‐dependent PK parameters [8].

In this manuscript, we describe population‐based mechanistic PK/PD modeling of TAK‐500 pharmacokinetics, receptor occupancy, and monocyte migration in cynomolgus monkeys. The population model captured the TMDD profiles of the total antibody and conjugated payload and estimated the payload deconjugation rate constant. To further project TAK‐500 PK and PD in humans, we leveraged previous TAK‐202 PK in humans to mitigate the uncertainties of TMDD PK translation between species. A similar modeling effort on TAK‐202 pharmacokinetics in cynomolgus monkeys confirmed that the PK properties of the TAK‐500 total antibody are comparable to those of TAK‐202, leading us to assume that the human PK profiles of TAK‐500 total antibody and TAK‐202 would likely be similar as well. The human PK of TAK‐500 conjugated payload was projected by assuming a similar deconjugation rate constant in cynomolgus monkeys and humans. This quantitative translation effort provides a unique example of using reverse translation to facilitate the clinical development of second‐generation biotherapeutics.

sec.title: Materials
sec.p: Murine antihuman CCR2 mAb (Mu1D9), humanized anti‐hCCR2 monoclonal antibody (TAK‐202), a mouse anti‐TAK‐202 idiotypic antibody, and TAK‐500, a TAK‐202‐derivative iADC conjugated to an interferon pathway agonist payload TAK‐676, were generated at Takeda Pharmaceuticals International Inc. (Cambridge, MA, USA). Blood samples were collected from healthy human donors and cynomolgus monkeys at Charles River Mattawan (Mattawan, MI, USA) and Charles River Ashland sites (Ashland, OH, USA), respectively. Whole blood was collected in sodium heparin tubes (158 USP units BD vacutainer blood collection tube; BD Biosciences, Franklin Lakes, NJ, USA). Lymphocyte count (absolute) and monocyte count (absolute) were evaluated from each human and cynomolgus monkey blood sample using the Advia 120 (Siemens Healthineers, Erlangen, Germany). All other reagents were obtained from commercial sources.

sec.title: In Vivo Studies
sec.p: All studies were conducted according to the study protocols approved by the Takeda Pharmaceuticals International Inc. Animal Care and Use Committee. PK blood samples were processed to plasma. Analysis of plasma samples was performed at Frontage Laboratories Inc. (Exton, PA) using qualified liquid chromatography with tandem mass spectrometry (LC–MS/MS) methods for total antibody (Total Ab), conjugated TAK‐676, and deconjugated TAK‐676 [3]. The lower limits of quantitation for the assays were 30.0 ng/mL for total Ab, 0.651 ng/mL for conjugated TAK‐676, and 0.500 ng/mL for deconjugated TAK‐676, respectively. Bioanalytical results were stored in Watson LIMS (version 7.4.1, Thermo Systems, Philadelphia, PA) and were reported to three significant figures. Concentration results for total Ab, conjugated TAK‐676, and deconjugated TAK‐676 that fell below the quantitation limit (BQL) for the respective analytes were reported in Watson as BQL and were treated as zero for statistical calculations.

sec.title: Pharmacokinetic/Pharmacodynamic Study of TAK‐500 in Cynomolgus Monkeys
sec.p: TAK‐500 was administered to three groups of protein therapeutic‐naïve female cynomolgus monkeys (2.6–4.5 kg, Charles River, Reno, AZ) at doses of 0.1 mg/kg (N = 4), 0.5 mg/kg (N = 4), and 3 mg/kg (N = 4) by slow bolus injection. Serial blood samples were collected into K2EDTA tubes from the femoral vein at predose and at 0, 0.83, 1, 6, 24, 72, 168, 240, 336, and 408 h post‐dose. A portion of whole blood samples was collected for CCR2 RO analysis. The remaining portions were centrifuged at 4°C (1500–2000× g), and resultant plasma samples were stored at −70°C until further analysis for drug concentrations.

sec.title: Noncompartmental Pharmacokinetic Analysis
sec.p: Noncompartmental analysis (NCA) was performed using Phoenix WinNonlin (Build 8.1.0.3530, Certara, L.P., Princeton, NJ, USA). All parameters were estimated using nominal dose levels and nominal sampling times relative to the start of dose administration, except when deviation to sampling time occurred; in such cases, the actual time was used. The concentration at time zero on Day 1 was back‐extrapolated based on the first two observed plasma concentrations, except for deconjugated TAK‐676, which was assumed to be zero for parameter estimation. Concentration values reported as BQL were assigned to a value of zero. The area under the concentration–time curve (AUC) was calculated using the linear up log down trapezoidal method. The AUC was not reported for PK profiles with fewer than three quantifiable concentrations at consecutive time points post‐dose. When practical, the terminal elimination phase of each concentration–time curve was identified using at least the final three observed concentration values. The slope of the terminal elimination phase was determined using log‐linear regression on the unweighted concentration data. Parameters relying on the determination of the terminal elimination phase were not reported if the Rsq was < 0.800, or if the %AUCextrap represented > 20% of the total area.

sec.title: Pharmacokinetic/Pharmacodynamic Study of TAK‐202 (Anti‐CCR2 mAb) in Cynomolgus Monkeys
sec.p: The pharmacokinetics and whole blood CCR2 receptor occupancy (RO) of TAK‐202 were investigated in cynomolgus monkeys. Three groups of three male (n = 3) and three female (n = 3) cynomolgus monkeys received a single slow IV infusion over 30 min of TAK‐202 at doses of 10, 30, or 100 mg/kg. Blood samples were collected for TAK‐202 analysis prior to treatment and at 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8, and 12 h after initiation of infusion on Day 1, and on Days 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 10, 12, 15, 19, 22, 29, and 36. Additional samples were collected to assess CCR2 RO on monocytes on Days −14, −7, and −1 prior to treatment, and at 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8, and 12 h after infusion on Day 1, and on Days 2, 3, 4, 5, 8, 10, 12, 15, 19, 22, 29, and 36. The concentrations of TAK‐202 were measured by the enzyme‐linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) method. ELISA was utilized for the quantitative determination of TAK‐202 concentrations in cynomolgus monkey serum samples. In this assay, a mouse anti‐TAK‐202 idiotypic antibody was incubated onto ELISA plates to which diluted test samples were added. After incubation, the unbound TAK‐202 was washed off and the bound TAK‐202 was detected by addition of a peroxidase mouse antihuman IgG conjugate solution. The plates were developed by addition of a colorimetric substrate solution. Data were reduced using the regression analysis program from SoftMax Pro (Molecular Devices), which employed a four‐parameter logistic model to fit the calibration curve and interpolate the sample results. The results were reported as μg/mL of serum. The lower limit of quantification (LLOQ) was 0.4 μg/mL.

sec.title: Quantification of CCR2 RO
sec.p: The extent of CCR2 RO in whole blood of human and cynomolgus monkey was determined using a direct RO assay. For in vitro human or cynomolgus monkey blood, samples (90 μL) were spiked with various known concentrations of mAbs to generate a dose curve up to saturating levels, followed by incubation at 4°C for 1 h. For in vivo cynomolgus monkey studies, samples were divided into two 90 μL aliquots; to one aliquot, a saturating TAK‐500 concentration was added, and both samples were incubated at 4°C for 1 h. After incubation, 1800 μL of 1× RBC lysis solution (ThermoFisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA) was added to each sample and mixed by pipetting. The samples were incubated at room temperature for 20 min in the dark and then centrifuged at 400× g for 5 min at 4°C. Cell pellets were resuspended with 100 μL of Live/Dead stain working solution (Live/Dead Fixable Near IR Dead Cell Stain solution; ThermoFisher Scientific) and incubated for 30 min at 4°C protected from light. The samples then were washed with 1800 μL of the stain buffer fetal bovine serum (FBS) (BD Biosciences), placed on ice, and incubated with 10 μL of Blocking Buffer Working Solution (BioXcell, Lebanon, NH, USA) for 10 min to block Fc‐mediated nonspecific binding. The samples were resuspended in 50 μL of either phycoerythrin (PE) staining cocktail containing detection antibody immunoglobulin (Ig)G‐PE and incubated for 30 min at 4°C protected from light. A background sample was generated by staining 1× PBS‐treated (in vitro) or baseline (in vivo) sample with all assay reagents in the absence of TAK‐500. The samples then were washed with 1800 μL of the stain buffer and resuspended in 50 μL of stain buffer containing HLA‐DR‐FITC, CD3‐PE‐Cy7, CD20‐PE‐Cy7, CD56‐PE‐Cy7, CD16‐APC, and CD14‐BV510 for human samples, and CD3‐PE‐Cy7, CD20‐PE‐Cy7, CD159a‐PE‐Cy7, CD16‐APC, and CD14‐BV510 was added for NHP samples and incubated for 30 min at 4°C protected from light. Following washing with 1800 μL of the stain buffer and centrifugation, the stained cells were resuspended in 500 μL stain buffer for flow cytometry analysis using BD FACSCanto II Flow Cytometry (BD Sciences). All flow cytometry data were analyzed using FACSDiva software (Version 8.0.1, BD Biosciences).

The percentage of CCR2 RO for the direct RO assay was calculated as follows: RO%=MFIsample−MFIbackgroundMFIsaturated sample−MFIbackground×100 where MFI was the median fluorescence intensity and saturated sample referred to the sample treated with a saturating concentration of ADC. For the EC50 calculation, %RO data versus drug concentration data were fitted with GraphPad Prism software (GraphPad Software Inc., San Diego, CA).

sec.title: TAK‐202 From Phase I Clinical Study
sec.p: TAK‐202 was administered as an intravenous infusion in a single ascending dose (SAD) study in healthy subjects. In this study, single doses of 0.1, 0.3, 1, 3, 6, and 10 mg/kg TAK‐202 (MLN1202) or placebo were administered to 48 healthy subjects via 1‐h intravenous infusions. In each of the six dose cohorts, eight healthy subjects were enrolled, of whom six received TAK‐202 and two received placebo. Dense pharmacokinetic sampling was conducted. Data were available from 36 subjects.

sec.title: Unbound CCR2 Quantification in Human Whole Blood
sec.p: An indirect CCR2 saturation assay was developed and qualified at the Esoterix Center for Clinical Trials Oncology/Cell Analysis (TECCT‐OCA). This assay assessed CCR2 RO on CD3+ T lymphocytes and CD14+ monocytes. The CCR2 saturation assay utilized a FITC‐conjugated murine antihuman CCR2 monoclonal antibody (mu1D9‐FITC) for detection of unbound (free) CCR2. Unlike monocytes, the fluorescence intensity (mean equivalent soluble fluorescence or MESF) of CCR2 was very low on CD3+ T lymphocytes due to low CCR2 expression. Therefore, CD3+ T lymphocytes were analyzed only for percent of cells positive for mu1D9‐FITC (free sites).

sec.title: Statistical Analysis and Reporting Conventions
sec.p: Sample size (N), arithmetic mean, median (minimum [min]—maximum [max]), standard deviation (SD), and coefficient of variation expressed as a percent (%CV), as well as mean ratios (Ab‐to‐ADC ratio) for appropriate grouping and sorting variables, were generated. The bioanalytical data, PK parameters, ratios, and descriptive statistics were reported to three significant figures, except the individual and/or median (Min—Max) T‐last values that were reported to generally align with the PK sampling times presented in the concentration tables, as well as the N, which was reported with no decimal.

sec.title: Pharmacokinetic/Pharmacodynamic Model of TAK‐500 in Cynomolgus Monkeys
sec.p:
A stepwise PK/PD model was built. PK of TAK‐500 in cynomolgus monkeys [1] was described by a 4‐compartment model (Figure 1, Equations (1), (2), (3), (4), (5), (6), (7), (8)). The structural model comprised A1 and A2, which represented the amount of conjugated antibody (ADC) in the central and peripheral compartments, respectively; A3 and A4 represented the amount of deconjugated antibody (Ab) in the central and peripheral compartments, respectively. The route of administration was modeled as a single IV bolus dose introduced to the A1 compartment. The plasma concentration of total antibody (s2) was the sum of the ADC and deconjugated antibody (Ab) concentrations. The plasma concentration of conjugated payload (s1) was the DAR adjusted ADC concentration (Equation 6). A proportional error model Equations (7) and (8) was included to account for the residual error. The biexponential profile of conjugated antibody was characterized using a 2‐compartment model with a linear elimination (kel) as well as a nonlinear receptor‐mediated clearance from the central compartment (Equations 1 and 2). The nonlinear clearance was captured using a Michaelis–Menten kinetic model with maximal elimination rate (V max) and drug concentration at 50% of maximal elimination rate (Km). The distribution of the ADC was parameterized by central volume of distribution (Vc) along with central and peripheral distribution rate constants (transfer rate constant from plasma to tissue [kpt] and transfer rate constant from tissue to plasma [ktp]). An additional first‐order rate constant, reported as “deconjugation rate constant,” was incorporated in the central compartment to characterize the deconjugation of the payload (TAK‐676) from the ADC to yield deconjugated antibody, as described in Figure 1, Equations (3) and (4). The disposition of the deconjugated antibody was assumed to be the same as the ADC. (1) dA1dt=−kel×A1−Vmax×A1Km×Vc+A1+A3−kpt×A1+ktp×A2−kdec×A1
(2) dA2dt=kpt×A1−ktp×A2

sec.title: Population PK/PD Modeling
sec.p: The population PK/PD modeling was performed using Phoenix WinNonlin (Build 8.1.0.3530, Certara, L.P., Princeton, NJ, USA). The stepwise population PK/PD model was run with the following parameters: algorithm—FOCE‐ELS; Stderr—Central Diff; method—Hessian; confidence level—95%; N—1000. Intersubject variability (η) was assessed using the omega block. Bootstrapping was done to assess the stability of the model with the same parameters listed above. Decision criteria during model development included judgment of model robustness and plausibility, inspection of goodness‐of‐fit plots, and evaluation of precision of parameter estimates.

sec.title: Two‐Compartment PK Modeling of TAK‐202 in Cynomolgus Monkeys
sec.p: The population PK of TAK‐202 in cynomolgus monkeys [2] was characterized by a 2‐compartment model with linear and nonlinear clearance (Figure 3, Equations 15 and 16). The route of administration was modeled as a single IV bolus dose introduced to the central compartment. The nonlinear clearance was captured using the Michaelis–Menten approximation of the CCR2‐TMDD model. The observed plasma concentration (Cp) from TAK‐202 was captured with the PK model (Equation 17). The structural model also included a residual error model on both Cp and RO to account for unexplained variability (Equation 18). The dose levels ranged from 100, 30, 10, 3, and 1 mg/kg. Intersubject variability (η) was assessed using the omega block. Bootstrapping was done to assess the stability of the model with the same parameters listed above. Decision criteria during model development included judgment of model robustness and plausibility, inspection of goodness‐of‐fit plots, and evaluation of precision of parameter estimates. (15) dA1dt=ktp×A2−kel×A1−Vmax×A1Km×Vc+A1−kpt×A1

sec.title: Two‐Compartment PK/RO Modeling of TAK‐202 in Human
sec.p:
The stepwise population PK/RO model of TAK‐202 in humans [3] was characterized by a 2‐compartment model with nonlinear clearance (Figure 4, Equations (19), (20), (21)). The route of administration was modeled as a 1‐h IV infusion introduced into the central compartment (A1). The nonlinear clearance was captured using the Michaelis–Menten approximation of the CCR2 TMDD kinetic model. The Cp was correlated with the CCR2 RO on total monocytes using an Emax model (Equation 22). The structural model also included a proportional residual error model on both Cp and RO to account for residual error (Equations 23 and 24). Intersubject variability (η) was assessed using the omega block. Bootstrapping was done to assess the stability of the model with the same parameters listed above. sec.title: TAK‐500 Human PK Projection
sec.p: Human PK of TAK‐500 was projected based on the assumptions that: (1) TAK‐500 had the same human PK total antibody PK as TAK‐202; (2) the kdec in human was assumed to be the same as that in monkey; and (3) TAK‐500 in clinical studies had a DAR of 4.6 (average). The human PK profiles at the proposed doses (50, 150, and 500 μg/kg) were simulated. The non‐compartmental PK parameters were estimated using Phoenix NLME 8.0 Software and were summarized in Table 3.

sec.title: Software
sec.p: TAK‐202 and TAK‐500 human PK projection were conducted using Phoenix NLME Software (Phoenix 8.0, Certara). Graphs included in this report were plotted using GraphPad Prism (Version 8.0.2; GraphPad Software Inc.). The molecular weight of TAK‐202, as well as the ADC antibody backbone, was 148,700 g/mol. The molecular weight of the ADC payload (TAK‐676) was 710.52 g/mol. The following unit conversion was used in the report: TAK‐202 or total Ab of ADC 1 μg/mL = 6.72 nM; Conjugated TAK‐676 1 μg/mL = 1.41 μM.

sec.title: Allometric Scaling to Estimate Kel, Ktp, Kpt, and Vc in Humans From Cynomolgus Monkeys
sec.p:
The human PK parameters, kel, ktp, kpt, and Vc of TAK‐202 were predicted from the corresponding parameters in cynomolgus monkeys using allometric scaling. The allometric scaling was executed by scaling the CL by an exponent of 0.85 and Vd with an exponent of 1 [9]. CLhuman=CLcynoBWhuman/BWcynow
Vdhuman=VdcynoBWhuman/BWcynow

sec.title: Compartment PK‐PD Model of TAK‐500 in Cynomolgus Monkeys
sec.p: The individual serum concentration‐time profiles (n = 4) of total Ab and conjugated TAK‐676 were analyzed following intravenous administration of TAK‐500 at 0.1, 0.5, and 3 mg/kg dose levels. Dose increments of 1:5:30 resulted in exposure increments of 1:8:56 for total Ab and 1:8:60 for conjugated TAK‐676 (Table 1). Hence, exposures (total Ab and conjugated TAK‐676) were observed to be greater than dose‐proportional, suggesting TMDD. The observed faster clearance (CL) of the conjugated payload, compared to total antibody, is reflective of ADC stability in circulation, leading to premature loss of payload over time. Furthermore, at doses of 0.1–0.5 mg/kg, the released payload in systemic circulation is minimal, so it remains below the bioanalytical limit of detection at all time points, and is only detectable at a few early timepoints following the 3 mg/kg IV dose.

caption.p: Mean pharmacokinetic parameters of TAK‐500 in cynomolgus monkeys after IV bolus administration.

fn.p: Abbreviations: AUCall, area under the curve until last time‐point; AUCINF, area under the curve until infinity; CL, clearance; C max, maximum serum concentration of the analyte in serum, measured in nM; SD, standard deviation; T 1/2, terminal half‐life; V ss, volume of distribution in central compartment in steady state.

sec.p: The TMDD pharmacokinetic (PK/RO/PD) model from cynomolgus primates was developed following intravenous administration of TAK‐500 at 0.1, 0.5, and 3 mg/kg (Figure 1). Nonlinear elimination was described using the Michaelis–Menten model. The population‐based compartment PK model (Figure 1A) described both the total antibody and conjugated payload profiles in serum following intravenous doses at 0.1, 0.5, and 3 mg/kg. The profiles of RO and whole blood monocytes were described using a stepwise fitting approach, which linked the serum concentration of the total antibody to CCR2 RO that subsequently led to the exit of monocytes from the circulation. Using this final model, the deconjugation rate constant (kdec) was estimated to be 0.0324 perhour at a fixed DAR of 4.6 (Table 2), corresponding to a deconjugation half‐life (T1/2) of 21 h, which was subsequently assumed to be similar in humans and applied in simulating the conjugated payload PK profiles in humans.

caption.p: Population estimates of cynomolgus monkey PK‐PD parameters of TAK‐500.

sec.title: TAK‐202 in Cynomolgus Monkeys
sec.p: The individual serum concentration‐time profiles (n = 6) of the CCR2‐mAb (TAK‐202) were analyzed following intravenous administration of TAK‐202 at 1, 3, 10, 30, and 100 mg/kg dose levels. Dose increments of 1:3:10:30:100 resulted in exposure increments of 1:10:32:94:210 for mAb, suggesting a greater than proportional increment in exposure due to the presence of TMDD (Table S2). The 2‐compartment Michaelis–Menten population PK model was developed to describe the TAK‐202 PK profiles in cynomolgus monkeys (Figure 2A). The population model captured the observed PK profile within the 5th and 95th percentiles of the simulations and closely overlayed with the median profile of the simulations (Figure 2C–E).

sec.title: Overlay of TAK‐202 and TAK‐500 PK Profiles in Cynomolgus Monkeys
sec.p: The TAK‐202 population PK model (Table S3) was applied to simulate profiles at low dose levels of 0.1, 0.5, and 3 mg/kg. This simulation showed a strong alignment between the observed total antibody profile of TAK‐500 and the model‐simulated TAK‐202 profiles (Figure 2C–E). The overlay indicated a high degree of PK similarity between the total antibody profile of TAK‐500 and the TAK‐202 profile in cynomolgus monkeys, suggesting comparable PK properties for the TAK‐500 total antibody and TAK‐202 in humans. These findings supported the projection of TAK‐500 total antibody PK in humans based on TAK‐202 profiles from clinical studies.

sec.title: TAK‐202 in Humans
sec.p: The individual serum concentration‐time profiles (n = 6/dose) of TAK‐202 in humans were analyzed following intravenous administration of TAK‐202 at 0.1, 0.3, 1, 3, 6, and 10 mg/kg dose levels (Figure 3A). Consistent with the observed monkey PK profiles, TAK‐202 exhibited more than dose‐proportional PK. Dose increments of 1:3:10:30:60:100 resulted in exposure increments of 1:5:35:158:410:937 for the mAb (Table S4). In addition, for TAK‐202 at dose levels of 0.1, 0.3, 1, 3, 6, and 10 mg/kg, estimated clearance (CL) was 1.19, 0.758, 0.325, 0.221, 0.179, and 0.125 mL/h/kg, demonstrating a lower clearance at higher dose levels (Table S4). The 2‐compartment population PK‐RO model (Table S5) with parallel linear and nonlinear elimination was developed to describe TAK‐202 PK profiles in humans following IV administration at 0.1, 0.3, 1, 3, 6, and 10 mg/kg dose levels. The population model also captured the CCR2‐RO using a maximal inhibitory response model (Figure 3B). The observed PK (Figure 3C–H) and RO (Figure 3I–N) profiles at all dose levels were well within the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of the simulations and closely overlaid with the median profile of the population simulations.

sec.title: TAK‐500 Human PK Projection
sec.p: The human PK of the TAK‐500 total antibody was assumed to be similar to that of the human TAK‐202 profile. However, the human PK profile of the TAK‐500 conjugate payload was projected by applying the TAK‐202 human PK parameters and incorporating the deconjugation rate constant (kdec = 0.03 h−1) estimated from the TAK‐500 Pop PK/RO/PD model in cynomolgus monkeys. The human PK profiles at the potential clinical doses (50, 150, and 500 μg/kg) were simulated using the established model (Figure 4). The estimated non‐compartmental PK parameters at each dose level were summarized in Table 3. Similar to TAK‐202 in humans, TAK‐500 was expected to demonstrate nonlinear PK in humans due to CCR2 TMDD. Within the projected clinical dose range (50 to 500 μg/kg), the model predicts decreasing clearance values with increasing dose, from 40 to 31 mL/h for total antibody and 148 to 124 mL/h for conjugated payload (median 70 kg adult), respectively. Accordingly, the terminal half‐life (T₁/₂) for the total antibody and conjugated payload was estimated to range from 114 to 118 h and 30 (9–41) to 60 (32–72) h, respectively (Table 3).

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: Chemokine receptors mediated the recruitment of immune cells to sites of inflammation and to tumors. The C‐C chemokine receptor type 2 (CCR2) is expressed by several bone marrow–derived cell types, including inflammatory monocytes, myeloid precursor cells, and immature dendritic cells, as well as B and T lymphocytes [10]. CCR2‐expressing cells are recruited primarily to inflammation by the C‐C chemokine ligand 2 (CCL2; [11]). Although other CCL family members also can activate CCR2. Chemotherapy treatment promotes CCR2‐dependent infiltration of tumor‐promoting myeloid cells into murine mammary tumors [12] and CCL2/CCR2–mediated recruitment of CCR2+ inflammatory monocytes to the lung has been shown to promote breast cancer extravasation and metastasis in mouse models [13, 14]. These findings sparked interest in targeting the CCR2 pathway to modulate the innate immune response for therapeutic benefit in cancer.

CCR2, a clinically tested target, shows correlation in patients with high CCR2 expression in breast cancer cells and shortened survival time compared with patients with low/negative CCR2 expression [15]. Additionally, an open‐label, nonrandomized Phase I trial using a CCR2 inhibitor against locally invasive pancreatic cancer suggested that the inhibitor enhanced chemotherapy response, reduced macrophage infiltration, and induced an anti‐tumor adaptive immune response [16]. With this approach, we aim to target the CCR2‐expressing cells by conjugating a STING‐payload to the anti‐CCR2 mAb. Therefore, we hypothesized that the TAK‐500 would not only block the CCR2/CCL2 mediated recruitment of the inflammatory monocytes to the tumor tissue but also facilitate the release of the STING‐payload (TAK‐676) within monocytes and immature dendritic cells thereby modulating the immune activation in the TME.

Clinical experience with mAb and antibody drug conjugates has grown over the past few decades. The characterization of their PK properties in cynomolgus monkeys and subsequent translation to humans has been well studied for antibodies that are predominantly cleared by catabolic metabolism [9]. In the case of antibodies that demonstrate significant TMDD, PK characterization in cynomolgus monkeys requires antibody concentration‐time profiles over a wide concentration range to capture saturation of target‐mediated clearance. This information can only be obtained if the test article is well tolerated in preclinical in vivo studies over a wide dose range. Besides, the challenges in characterizing the nonlinearity, the translation of the nonlinearity between cynomolgus monkeys to humans is an unknown. To predict human PK of antibodies that undergo TMDD, the nonlinear PK models such as Michaelis–Menten (MM) or full TMDD model are developed, and the species differences in terms of target expression levels, binding affinity, turnover of the target, internalization of the bound receptor‐drug complex are also considered. In an alternative approach, the scale‐up of the nonlinear clearance from preclinical species to humans with anti‐CD33 ADC in AML patients was described [17]. In this report, Km, the concentration driving the half‐maximal nonlinear clearance among the preclinical species was found to be comparable to the binding affinity (KD) of the ADC to the CD33 target. Hence, for human prediction, the difference in binding affinity between cynomolgus monkey and human was used as a factor to project nonlinear clearance in humans. However, this scaling of Km comes with the assumption that binding affinity is the rate limiting step in humans as observed in cynomolgus monkeys, which may lead to errors in clinical projections [18]. In addition, the clinically relevant V max was projected by estimating the extent of non‐dose proportionality in C max of nonhuman primate vs. human from surrogate anti‐CD33 mAb. Yet again, this approach is utilized in case of clinically validated targets, targets that are abundantly expressed in circulation and with drug candidates that have a wide therapeutic index.

In this report, we conducted in vivo studies to characterize the PK‐PD of TAK‐500 in cynomolgus monkeys. A population PK model was further developed to describe the overlay of the anti‐CCR2 monoclonal antibody (TAK‐202) to the total antibody component of the ADC (TAK‐500) in cynomolgus monkeys. It is assumed that the catabolic antibody clearance is independent of the DAR, which is supported by our observation that the PK of TAK‐500 total antibody was comparable with that of TAK‐202 in cynomolgus monkeys. This is consistent with the observation by others that there was a similar PK and tissue distribution of an ADC in a cleavable linker format with DAR ≤ 5.8 [19]. In addition, without PK characterization of individual DAR species, there is insufficient data to estimate DAR‐dependent antibody clearance.

The Phase I anti‐CCR2 mAb (TAK‐202) PK data was available at dose levels of 0.1, 0.3, 1, 3, 6 and 10 mg/kg [20, 21]. We compared the PK parameters of the anti‐CCR2 mAb from cynomolgus monkeys vs. humans and observed a~13 fold faster nonlinear clearance in humans vs. cynomolgus monkeys (Tables S1–S5). Due to differences in physiochemical properties of mAb and ADC, allometrically scaling the linear clearance with an exponent of 0.85 and Vd with an exponent of 1.0 [6, 9], led to underprediction of TAK‐202 human PK at 10 mg/kg (Figure S4). we observe a moderate overprediction of TAK‐202 human exposure at low dose levels such as 0.1 and 0.3 mg/kg, most likely due to faster nonlinear clearance in humans vs. cynomolgus monkeys, at a dose range where TMDD is expected to be more prominent.

Due to these challenges in allometrically scaling the PK, we utilized clinical PK parameters of the anti‐CCR2 mAb (TAK‐202) disposition to project the anti‐CCR2‐iADC (TAK‐500) total antibody profile in humans. The projected TAK‐500 PK was derived from the clinical profile of the parental mAb (TAK‐202) in healthy volunteers. However, this projection carries inherent limitations: (1) Non‐linear clearance at lower dose levels may differ across various disease populations (e.g., healthy volunteers vs. solid tumors) due to differences in target abundance among these cohorts; (2) The V max/Km approximation was applied to account for the nonlinearity. However, at lower dose levels, where the target concentration significantly exceeds drug concentration, the Michaelis–Menten approximation may not fully capture the extent of nonlinearity. Given that only drug concentrations were measured but not receptor concentrations, the use of the Michaelis–Menten approximation was used as a simplification to avoid over‐parameterization. As for the projection of the conjugated payload profile of TAK‐500 in humans, the simulations were shown by assuming a similar deconjugation rate constant between cynomolgus monkeys and humans (Figure 1).

Finally, with the PK‐RO human simulations we observe a faster deconjugation rate (0.03 1/h) vs. elimination rate (0.002 1/h). This can be observed in the simulated profiles of the conjugated payload and total antibody crossover at 72 h. The faster deconjugation rate may suggest a potential loss of payload from the ADC, with higher levels of deconjugated antibody potentially competing with anti‐CCR2‐iADC (TAK‐500) for binding to the CCR2 receptors. The modeling suggests the need for a more frequent dosing regimen to maintain pharmacological activity. However, the optimal clinical regimen should also consider available and emerging safety information as well as operational feasibility. Thereby, these simulations enabling forward translation from cynomolgus monkeys to humans facilitate a initial plan for phase I clinical study. The performance of the developed PK/PD model for TAK‐500 will be further evaluated against clinical data once available.
